description: The chart shows how many hateful-communication datasets were published each year from 2012 to 2022, broken down by researcher location for five named locations plus an “Other” category. The horizontal axis lists the categories as years in chronological order from 2012 through 2022 and is labeled “Year.” The vertical axis is labeled “Number of datasets” and uses a logarithmic (exponential) scale with major ticks at approximately \(10^0\), \(10^1\), and \(10^2\) (about 1, 10, and 100), spanning roughly from 1 up to a little over 100. Bars are grouped by year, with up to six colored bars per year corresponding to the legend “Researcher Location”: Other (blue), USA (orange), IN (green), UK (red), IT (purple), and DE (brown). Approximate values by year are: 2012 shows USA at about 2; 2013 shows USA at about 2; 2014 shows Other about 2 and USA about 1; 2015 shows Other about 3 and DE about 1; 2016 shows Other about 4, USA about 7, IN about 3, and UK about 2; 2017 shows Other about 18, USA about 14, IN about 1, UK about 9, and IT about 5; 2018 shows Other about 30, USA about 12, IN about 4, UK about 4, and DE about 4; 2019 shows Other about 50, USA about 16, IN about 6, UK about 2, and IT about 8; 2020 shows Other about 85, USA about 40, IN about 12, UK about 15, IT about 2, and DE about 18; 2021 shows Other about 110, USA about 45, IN about 22, UK about 17, IT about 12, and DE about 9; and 2022 shows Other about 25, USA about 3, IN about 9, UK about 8, and IT about 1 (with no visible DE bar). The bars are not sorted by height within each year, and there are no special visual emphases such as outlines or annotations beyond the legend and axis labeling.
caption_used: The bar chart illustrates the distribution of datasets over time for the five most frequent researcher locations and all other locations combined, spanning the years 2012 to 2022. The horizontal axis represents the years, while the vertical axis indicates the number of datasets on an exponential scale ranging from 10^0 to 10^2. Researchers from the USA consistently published the highest number of datasets across all years, with a peak in 2020. Notably, researchers from India surpassed those from the UK in dataset production in 2021, marking a significant shift in contributions. Additionally, the number of datasets from Germany declined steadily after 2018, indicating reduced activity in dataset production from this region.
